title: History: How the Past Is Known
description: How historians turn traces into accounts: sources, evidence, time, cause and interpretation, learned through well-chosen cases from the ancient world to 1914. A first course; later courses cover periods and regions in depth.
audience: A curious adult with no special background. They have heard of Rome, the Reformation and the First World War but have not been taught how historians know what they know.
outcomes: You'll be able to say what a source is evidence of, and weigh it by who made it and why.
You'll be able to place events on a timeline and compute intervals across the BCE/CE boundary.
You'll be able to separate the conditions, causes and trigger of an event.
You'll be able to tell a fact from an interpretation and see why historians differ.
You'll be able to build a qualified historical claim and name what would weaken it.

modules.title: Sources and evidence
modules.summary: A source is a trace left by people with their own reasons. Three ancient cases show how to ask what a source can and cannot tell us.

modules.title: Time, numbers and cause
modules.summary: Placing events on a timeline, counting what a record counted, and separating the causes of an event from its conditions and its trigger.

modules.title: Interpretation and voice
modules.summary: Why historians disagree about the same evidence, how an event's meaning changes after it, and whose voices the surviving record leaves out.

modules.title: Argument across the long run
modules.summary: Cause at the scale of a world war, building a historical claim from evidence, and a map of the whole spine that later period courses will fill.

lessons.title: What a source is
lessons.objective: Say what a source is evidence of, and classify a source as primary or secondary for a particular question.

concepts.title: Source
concepts.summary: Anything made or left by people that a historian uses as evidence about the past.

concepts.title: Primary source
concepts.summary: A source made at the time being studied, or by someone who took part in it.

concepts.title: Secondary source
concepts.summary: A later account built from other sources.

misconceptions: Taking a source to be a window onto the past rather than something made by someone for a reason.
Assuming primary means true and secondary means unreliable; neither follows.
Thinking a source is primary or secondary in itself, when it depends on the question being asked.
sequence: Open on the Rosetta Stone and ask what a slab of stone could tell us, and about what.
Show that it is a copy of a decree issued at Memphis in 196 BCE in the name of Ptolemy V, written in three scripts.
Distinguish what it is evidence of: the decree's content, the priests who issued it, and the way the Ptolemies ruled Egypt.
Classify: for the decree it is primary; a 2020 book about Ptolemaic Egypt is secondary; the same book is primary for how historians in 2020 wrote.
Make the point that the category belongs to the question, not the object.
examples: The Rosetta Stone carries one decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek. French soldiers found it in July 1799 near Rashid (Rosetta) in the Nile delta; it passed to Britain in 1801 and has been in the British Museum since 1802. Jean-François Champollion announced his decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822. For a question about Ptolemy V's relations with the priests, the stone is primary. For a question about how Europeans came to read hieroglyphs, the stone is evidence of a different kind, and Champollion's 1822 letter is primary.

figures.shows: A timeline from 200 BCE to 1830 CE with three events: Memphis decree (-196), stone found at Rosetta (1799), Champollion announces decipherment (1822). Event details are shown after the learner places each one.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the year marker to each event and read its note; then order the three by date.
figures.placement: Ties the object to the three moments in its story.

figures.shows: A photograph-style drawing of the stone with three bands labelled by script; the band meanings are hidden until chosen.
figures.learnerAction: Tap each band to see its script and which of the three the reader of the time would have read.

questionPlan.sample: For a question about how Ptolemaic rulers dealt with Egyptian priests, the Rosetta Stone decree is:
questionPlan.answer: A primary source

questionPlan.sample: Which statement about primary sources is correct?
questionPlan.answer: They were made at the time but can still be wrong or one-sided
choices: They were made at the time but can still be wrong or one-sided

questionPlan.sample: Put in date order: Champollion announces his decipherment; the Memphis decree is issued; soldiers find the stone.
questionPlan.answer: Memphis decree (196 BCE), stone found (1799), decipherment announced (1822)

historyNotes: The decree dates to 196 BCE and was issued at Memphis for Ptolemy V; found 1799 by French soldiers; British Museum since 1802; Champollion 1822. Check the exact find date and the day of the decree before quoting.

lessons.title: Who made it, for whom and why
lessons.objective: Source a text by asking who made it, for whom, when and why, and say what that implies for how far to trust each part.

concepts.title: Sourcing
concepts.summary: Asking who made a source, when, for what audience and for what purpose before asking what it says.

concepts.title: Purpose and audience
concepts.summary: The reason a source was made and the reader it was made for, which shape what it includes and leaves out.

concepts.title: Corroboration
concepts.summary: Checking a claim in one source against other, independent sources.

misconceptions: Judging a source only by whether its content sounds plausible, without asking who made it.
Treating an official statement as neutral, or an account by an opponent as automatically false.
Thinking that two sources that agree have corroborated each other when one copied the other.
sequence: Introduce Augustus's Res Gestae: a record of his achievements, set up on bronze pillars at his mausoleum after his death in 14 CE.
Ask the sourcing questions: who made it (Augustus, or those carrying out his instructions), for whom (the people of Rome), why (to fix how he would be remembered).
Set it beside Tacitus's Annals, written about a century later, which begins with Augustus's death and rule, and ask what each is good evidence for.
Show what corroboration looks like when a claim is in both, and what it looks like when only one source makes it.
Close on the idea that bias is not a reason to discard a source; it is a reason to ask a better question of it.
examples: The best-preserved copy of the Res Gestae is an inscription from Ancyra (modern Ankara), in Latin with a Greek version. Tacitus wrote the Annals in the early second century CE and opens by saying kings first held the city of Rome. Question: how many years after Augustus's death in 14 CE did Tacitus write, if he was working about 116 CE? 102. The Res Gestae is excellent evidence of how Augustus wished to be seen and weak evidence of how contemporaries saw him.

figures.shows: Two columns, Res Gestae and Annals, with rows for author, date, audience, purpose; the cells are filled in by the learner from short extracts.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the right cell into each row of the sourcing table.

questionPlan.sample: The Res Gestae was made to record Augustus's achievements. It is best evidence of:
questionPlan.answer: How Augustus wanted to be remembered
choices: How ordinary Romans felt about him
How Augustus wanted to be remembered

questionPlan.sample: Augustus died in 14 CE and Tacitus wrote the Annals about 116 CE. How many years apart is that?
Two accounts agree on a claim, but one is known to have copied the other. Does the agreement corroborate the claim?
questionPlan.answer: No: they are not independent

historyNotes: Augustus died on 19 August 14 CE. The Res Gestae survives mainly as the copy at Ancyra (the Monumentum Ancyranum). Verify the dates of Tacitus's Annals; the early second century is safe.

lessons.title: Silences, survival and one-sided records
lessons.objective: Explain how survival and silence shape what we can know, and treat a number in a hostile source with care.

concepts.title: Survival
concepts.summary: What reaches us is not what existed but what was kept, copied or buried in the right way.

concepts.title: Silence
concepts.summary: The absence of a voice or a topic in the record, which can be a fact about the past or only about the evidence.

concepts.title: Source written by an enemy
concepts.summary: A source whose author fought, or wrote for people who fought, against the people described.

misconceptions: Reading no evidence as evidence of absence: a thing missing from the record may have gone unrecorded or been lost.
Believing the winners always write the history; the survivors often do, but so do those who happened to be literate.
Rejecting a hostile source wholesale instead of using it for what the author could have known.
sequence: Describe the Persian Wars as we know them: Greek accounts, above all Herodotus writing in the fifth century BCE, narrate Marathon in 490 BCE and Thermopylae and Salamis in 480 BCE.
Ask where the Persian side is: royal inscriptions such as Darius I's at Behistun, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, record deeds and not wars with Greece.
Work through a number: Herodotus gives Xerxes's army as 1,700,000 infantry; ask what we can check it against, and what the number does for his story.
Distinguish what a hostile author can know (what his own side did) from what he has reasons to inflate.
State the rule: ask what a silence is a silence of.
examples: Herodotus gives a figure of 1,700,000 infantry for Xerxes's army; modern historians put the real figure far lower. Classify the claim: a hostile, uncorroborated number that serves the author's story that Greece faced overwhelming odds.

figures.shows: A timeline from 530 BCE to 470 BCE: Darius I's inscription at Behistun (about -520), Marathon (-490), Thermopylae and Salamis (-480), Plataea (-479). Whose record survives for each is shown after placement.
figures.learnerAction: Place each event, then tap to see which side's evidence survives.
figures.placement: What survived is not what happened.

questionPlan.sample: The Persian court left no narrative of the war with Greece. What follows?
questionPlan.answer: Nothing certain: the silence may be loss or choice
choices: The wars did not matter to Persia
Nothing certain: the silence may be loss or choice

questionPlan.sample: Herodotus says 1,700,000 infantry. What is the sound way to treat the number?
questionPlan.answer: As a claim to test, not a fact to count
choices: As a fact because he was there
As a claim to test, not a fact to count
As an exact record from Persian files

questionPlan.sample: Order: Marathon; Plataea; Thermopylae and Salamis.
questionPlan.answer: Marathon (490 BCE), Thermopylae and Salamis (480 BCE), Plataea (479 BCE)

historyNotes: Darius I's Behistun inscription dates from the 520s BCE; Marathon 490 BCE; Thermopylae and Salamis 480 BCE; Plataea 479 BCE. Behistun carries Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian texts.

lessons.title: Dates, eras and periods
lessons.objective: Compute intervals across the BCE/CE boundary, name the century of a year, and say why a period boundary is a judgement.

concepts.title: BCE and CE
concepts.summary: Years counted back from, and forward from, the traditional date of Jesus's birth; there is no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE.

concepts.title: Century
concepts.summary: The 5th century CE is 401 to 500; the 5th century BCE is 500 to 401 BCE.

concepts.title: Periodisation
concepts.summary: Dividing the past into named stretches such as 'ancient' and 'medieval', which are labels chosen by later people.

misconceptions: Computing 44 BCE to 14 CE as 58 years, forgetting there is no year 0.
Calling 1453 'the 14th century' because the digits begin 14.
Treating a period name as something people at the time used, as if they knew they were 'medieval'.
sequence: Lay out one axis on which BCE years count down to 1 BCE and CE years count up from 1 CE, with nothing between them.
Compute an interval across the boundary: 44 BCE to 14 CE is 43 + 14 = 57 years (to 1 BCE is 43, plus 14).
Name centuries: 476 is in the 5th century, 1453 in the 15th, 490 BCE in the 5th BCE.
Take two dates for the end of Rome: 476 (Romulus Augustulus deposed by Odoacer) and 1453 (Constantinople to Mehmed II), and the 977 years between them.
Say what the choice of boundary argues for.
examples: Caesar was assassinated in 44 BCE and Augustus died in 14 CE: 43 + 14 = 57 years. 1453 - 476 = 977 years between the deposition of Romulus Augustulus and the fall of Constantinople. The 1st century BCE is 100 to 1 BCE.

figures.shows: An axis from 500 BCE to 1500 CE with the events -44, 14, 476 and 1453. The learner must tap the boundary they would use for 'end of the ancient world' before the labels appear.
figures.learnerAction: Move the boundary marker and watch the period labels change.

questionPlan.sample: How many years from 44 BCE to 14 CE?
How many years from 476 CE to 1453 CE?
In which century is 1453?
questionPlan.answer: The 15th century

historyNotes: Julius Caesar was assassinated on 15 March 44 BCE; Romulus Augustulus was deposed in 476 CE; Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453.

lessons.title: Counting the past: records that count
lessons.objective: Say what a record of counting actually counted, and use it with care for questions it was not built to answer.

concepts.title: Purpose of a record
concepts.summary: A tally is made to answer a particular question for its makers, such as who owes tax, and counts what that question needs.

concepts.title: Estimate
concepts.summary: A number reached by reasoning from partial evidence, which should be given with its range.

concepts.title: Proxy
concepts.summary: A measurable thing used to stand in for something not recorded directly.

misconceptions: Treating an old count as a census in the modern sense, when it recorded only what its makers valued.
Quoting one estimate as if it were the figure, ignoring the stated range.
Assuming a figure is exact because it is precise.
sequence: Introduce Domesday Book: William I ordered a survey at Christmas 1085, and the results were written up in 1086.
Ask what it counts: landholders, manors, ploughlands, tenants, values; ask what it omits.
Show the difference between 'the survey recorded N households' and 'England had N people'.
Do an estimate with a multiplier and show how the range moves with the assumption.
Contrast with the Black Death: no single count exists, so mortality is a range from several sources.
examples: A survey records 1,200 households in a town and historians assume 4 to 5 people per household: 4,800 to 6,000 people. A hypothetical town of 4,000 with 40% mortality loses 1,600; with 30% it loses 1,200. Estimates for the Black Death in Europe are usually given as a range, not a number.

figures.shows: A mock page from a tax survey with rows for place, landholder, ploughlands, value; columns the learner can mark as 'counted' or 'not counted'.
figures.learnerAction: Mark which things the survey counted and which it left out.

questionPlan.sample: A survey records 1,200 households. At 4 people per household, how many people is that?
At 5 people per household?
A tax survey lists landholders and values. A question it can best answer is:
questionPlan.answer: Who held land and what it was worth for tax
choices: Who held land and what it was worth for tax

historyNotes: William I ordered the survey at Christmas 1085; Domesday Book was compiled in 1086; it exists in Great and Little Domesday volumes. The Black Death reached Messina in 1347. Household multipliers are conventional and debated.

lessons.title: Causes, conditions and triggers
lessons.objective: Separate the conditions, causes and trigger of an event and test a cause by asking what would have changed without it.

concepts.title: Condition
concepts.summary: A background state that made an event possible without making it happen.

concepts.title: Trigger
concepts.summary: The event that set off something already likely.

concepts.title: Counterfactual test
concepts.summary: Asking what would likely have happened if one factor had been absent, to judge how much it mattered.

misconceptions: Treating the nearest event as the cause because it came last.
Looking for one cause when events have several that work together.
Using a counterfactual as a story rather than a test of how likely the event was without the factor.
sequence: Pose the question: did printing cause the Reformation?
Lay out facts: Jan Hus burned at Constance in 1415; Gutenberg's Bible about 1455; Luther's Ninety-five Theses in 1517; Luther before the Diet of Worms in 1521.
Compare: Hus's ideas spread without print and were suppressed; Luther's reached many readers in print within years.
Sort the factors into conditions (print, discontent, political rivalries), cause (Luther's argument and princes' protection) and trigger (indulgence sale).
Make the point that a factor can be necessary without being enough.
examples: Order: Hus burned 1415, Gutenberg Bible about 1455, Ninety-five Theses 1517, Luther at Worms 1521. 1517 - 1415 = 102 years between Hus's death and the Theses. Print is a condition that widened Luther's audience; without it the same argument might have been contained as Hus's was.

figures.shows: Four event cards: Hus burned; Gutenberg Bible; Ninety-five Theses; Luther at Worms.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the cards into date order.
figures.placement: A chain of conditions, causes and triggers.

questionPlan.sample: Order: Ninety-five Theses; Hus burned at Constance; Luther at Worms; Gutenberg Bible.
questionPlan.answer: Hus (1415), Gutenberg Bible (about 1455), Ninety-five Theses (1517), Worms (1521)

questionPlan.sample: Printing made it possible for Luther's pamphlets to reach many readers. In the sort of conditions, causes and triggers, print is mainly:
questionPlan.answer: A condition

questionPlan.sample: How many years between Hus's death in 1415 and the Ninety-five Theses in 1517?

historyNotes: Hus was burned on 6 July 1415; Gutenberg's Bible dates to about 1455; Luther's Theses are traditionally dated 31 October 1517 although the posting is disputed; the Diet of Worms was in April 1521.

lessons.title: Why historians disagree
lessons.objective: Separate a claim of fact from an interpretation and say what in a debate is about evidence and what is about weighing it.

concepts.title: Interpretation
concepts.summary: An account that selects facts and weighs them to explain what happened.

concepts.title: Historiography
concepts.summary: The history of how historians have written about a topic.

concepts.title: Presentism
concepts.summary: Judging the past by present concerns as if people then shared them.

misconceptions: Believing that if historians disagree, no view is better than another.
Treating a fact such as a date and a judgement such as 'decline' as the same kind of claim.
Assuming each new generation merely corrects the last, when new questions also change what counts as evidence.
sequence: Ask what happened to the Roman West after 476.

Give three readings: Edward Gibbon (first volume of The Decline and Fall, 1776) emphasised decay and the effects of Christianity; Peter Brown (The World of Late Antiquity, 1971) emphasised transformation; Bryan Ward-Perkins (2005) argued from archaeology for real material collapse.
Show which statements each shares (476 as a date) and which separate them (what 'decline' means).
Show how the evidence invites different readings: pottery, buildings, coin finds.
State what makes one interpretation stronger: how much of the evidence it covers, and how well it deals with what does not fit.
examples: Classify: 'Romulus Augustulus was deposed in 476' (fact); 'Rome fell because it lost civic virtue' (interpretation); 'fine pottery disappears from most of Britain by the 5th century' (evidence offered for a reading). The three books are 1776, 1971 and 2005.

figures.shows: Three shelves labelled with the dates 1776, 1971 and 2005, and a tray of statements about the end of the Roman West.
figures.learnerAction: Sort each statement into fact, evidence or interpretation; the shelves show which reading uses which.

questionPlan.sample: 'Rome declined because it lost civic virtue.' This is:
questionPlan.answer: An interpretation

questionPlan.sample: 'Romulus Augustulus was deposed in 476.' This is:
questionPlan.answer: A fact claim (dated)

questionPlan.sample: Order the books: Ward-Perkins; Gibbon vol. 1; Brown.
questionPlan.answer: Gibbon (1776), Brown (1971), Ward-Perkins (2005)

historyNotes: Gibbon's first volume appeared in 1776; Brown's The World of Late Antiquity in 1971; Ward-Perkins's The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization in 2005.

lessons.title: What it meant then and what it has meant since
lessons.objective: Distinguish what a document did in its own time from the later uses made of it, and judge its significance.

concepts.title: Significance
concepts.summary: How much an event matters, judged against a stated question and a stated audience.

concepts.title: Afterlife
concepts.summary: The later uses and meanings given to an event or text, often different from what it did at the time.

concepts.title: Anachronism
concepts.summary: Placing a later idea, word or thing in an earlier time.

misconceptions: Reading a charter as a statement of modern rights because later people used it that way.
Treating significance as a single fact about an event, when it depends on who is asking and why.
Dismissing an afterlife as untrue; it is a real part of history even when it differs from the original.
sequence: Magna Carta, sealed by King John at Runnymede on 15 June 1215.
Show what it did then: a settlement with rebel barons, soon annulled by Pope Innocent III in August 1215.
Show what it came to be: reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225, and confirmed in 1297; in the 17th century lawyers such as Sir Edward Coke used it against the Stuart kings.
Ask about significance: significance to whom, for what question.
Contrast the document's life in weeks with its life in centuries.
examples: Order: sealed 1215; reissued 1225; confirmed by Edward I 1297. Years between 1215 and 1297: 82. Its first life lasted about ten weeks before the Pope annulled it (15 June to August), but its reissues made it the base of later claims.

figures.shows: A timeline 1200 to 1700: sealed 1215, annulled 1215, reissued 1225, confirmed 1297, used by Coke in 17th-century disputes (about 1628). Notes appear on click.
figures.learnerAction: Place events, then pick the one that most changed the charter's future.

questionPlan.sample: How many years from the sealing of Magna Carta in 1215 to its confirmation in 1297?
In 1215 Magna Carta mainly was:
questionPlan.answer: A settlement with rebel barons that soon failed
choices: A settlement with rebel barons that soon failed

questionPlan.sample: Rate how well you could explain why Magna Carta matters more now than in 1216, in two sentences.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated 1 to 5

historyNotes: Sealed 15 June 1215 at Runnymede; annulled by Innocent III in August 1215; reissued 1216, 1217, 1225; confirmed 1297 by Edward I; Coke and the Petition of Right (1628) in the 17th century.

lessons.title: Whose voices survive
lessons.objective: Read a record for the voices it contains and omits, and say how historians work with a thin or one-sided record.

concepts.title: Missing voices
concepts.summary: People who shaped events but left little in writing or were recorded only by others.

concepts.title: Reading against the grain
concepts.summary: Using a source for something its author did not mean to show.

concepts.title: Oral and later testimony
concepts.summary: Memory handed down or recorded later, valuable and different in its limits from a contemporary document.

misconceptions: Concluding that people who left no writing had no views or agency.
Using only the official record because it is the largest.
Treating oral or later testimony as worse than written, rather than different.
sequence: Set out the Haitian Revolution: an uprising in Saint-Domingue in August 1791; abolition proclaimed there in 1793; the French Convention abolished slavery in 1794; Napoleon's attempt to restore it in 1802; independence declared on 1 January 1804.
Ask who left records: planters, colonial officials, newspapers, Toussaint Louverture's letters, and few written by the enslaved themselves.
Show reading against the grain: a planter's list of lost property tells us about those who ran.
Show the problem with famous scenes such as Bois Caïman, known from later accounts.
Draw the lesson: a record's gaps are part of what we say about the past.
examples: Order: uprising August 1791; abolition by the Convention 1794; Napoleon's restoration attempt 1802; independence 1 January 1804. 1804 - 1791 = 13 years from the uprising to independence.

figures.shows: A timeline 1785 to 1810 with 1791 uprising, 1794 abolition decree, 1802 restoration attempt, 1804 independence. Each event shows whose records exist.
figures.learnerAction: Place the events, then mark the voices the record contains.
figures.placement: Years of revolution, voices of the record.

questionPlan.sample: How many years between the August 1791 uprising and independence in 1804?
A planter's letter complaining that workers have left the estate is best used to learn:
questionPlan.answer: That workers were acting on their own, though its author did not mean to say so
choices: That workers were acting on their own, though its author did not mean to say so

questionPlan.sample: Order: independence declared; the Convention abolishes slavery; Napoleon tries to restore it; uprising begins.
questionPlan.answer: Uprising (1791), abolition (1794), restoration attempt (1802), independence (1804)

historyNotes: The uprising began on the night of 22 to 23 August 1791; the Convention abolished slavery on 4 February 1794; Napoleon's law restoring slavery is dated 1802; independence was declared on 1 January 1804. Toussaint Louverture died in 1803 in French custody.

lessons.title: One war, many causes
lessons.objective: Order the events of the July crisis and sort long-term causes from short-term causes and the trigger.

concepts.title: Long-term cause
concepts.summary: A standing condition built up over years, such as alliances or rivalries.

concepts.title: Short-term cause
concepts.summary: A decision or event close in time to the outcome.

concepts.title: Contingency
concepts.summary: The idea that events could have gone otherwise because people chose and chance played a part.

misconceptions: Blaming one assassin or one alliance for a war.
Assuming that because a war was likely, it was inevitable.
Putting the sequence of events in order of importance instead of date.
sequence: Fix the sequence: the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914; Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia on 28 July; Germany declares war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August; Britain declares war on Germany on 4 August after the German invasion of Belgium.
Sort factors as long-term (alliances, arms and naval rivalry, nationalism), short-term (the July crisis decisions) and trigger (Sarajevo).
Apply the counterfactual test: how likely was a general war without Sarajevo, and how would the same crisis have played had one decision been different?
Introduce contingency: likely is not inevitable.
Have the learner write a one-line claim, with its weakest point.
examples: Sequence by date: 28 June, 28 July, 1 August, 3 August, 4 August 1914. Interval from the assassination to Britain's declaration: 28 June to 4 August is 37 days (2 days to 30 June, 31 in July, 4 in August).

figures.shows: Five event cards for the crisis.
figures.placement: The July crisis as a chain.

questionPlan.sample: How many days from 28 June to 4 August 1914?
Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 is best classed as:
questionPlan.answer: The trigger

questionPlan.sample: Order: Britain declares war; Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia; Sarajevo assassination; Germany declares war on Russia.
questionPlan.answer: Sarajevo, Austria-Hungary on Serbia, Germany on Russia, Britain

historyNotes: 28 June 1914 Sarajevo; 28 July Austria-Hungary on Serbia; 1 August Germany on Russia; 3 August Germany on France; 4 August Britain on Germany. Confirm these before use.

lessons.title: Building a historical claim
lessons.objective: Turn a question into a qualified claim, choose the evidence that supports it, and say what evidence would weaken it.

concepts.title: Claim
concepts.summary: A statement that answers the historical question and can be argued with evidence.

concepts.title: Qualification
concepts.summary: A limit on a claim, such as 'in Britain' or 'mainly', that keeps it as strong as the evidence allows.

concepts.title: Counter-evidence
concepts.summary: Evidence a claim has to explain or concede.

misconceptions: Writing a claim that cannot be wrong, such as 'many things caused it'.
Piling up evidence that does not bear on the claim.
Hiding evidence that cuts the other way instead of dealing with it.
sequence: Take a question: why did industrial change come early to Britain?

Lay out a dated sequence of developments: Darby's coke smelting at Coalbrookdale, 1709; Newcomen's steam engine, 1712; Watt's patent for a separate condenser, 1769; the Stockton and Darlington Railway, 1825.
Draft a claim and test it: is it narrow enough to be wrong?
Choose evidence that bears on the claim (cheap coal, high wages) and set aside what does not.
Add a qualifier and name a piece of counter-evidence.
examples: Weak: 'Industrialisation had many causes.' Better: 'Britain industrialised early because coal was cheap and wages were high, which made machines pay.' Evidence order: 1709, 1712, 1769, 1825. 1825 - 1712 = 113 years from the first engine to the first public steam railway.

lessons.title: The spine: a map of the past
lessons.objective: Place the course's case studies on one timeline, see the long-run threads, and choose a period to study next.

concepts.title: Spine
concepts.summary: A chain of dated events and eras that lets later study hang off a fixed frame.

concepts.title: Thread
concepts.summary: A theme traced across many periods, such as writing, states, trade or belief.

concepts.title: Scale
concepts.summary: The size of the time or place a claim is about, which changes what evidence counts.

misconceptions: Memorising dates without a frame in which they connect.
Assuming Europe's sequence is the world's.
Mixing scales: using one event to prove a claim about an era.
sequence: Lay out the cases: 490 BCE Marathon; 196 BCE decree; 14 CE Augustus; 476; 1086 Domesday; 1215 Magna Carta; 1517 Theses; 1791 uprising; 1914.
Assign each to a method: sources, sourcing, silence, time, counting, cause, interpretation, voice.
Trace a thread such as 'who writes records' through the cases.
Show what the follow-on courses would add: regional and period depth.
End with a self-rated review of the method steps.
examples: The span from the first to last case: from 490 BCE to 1914 is 490 + 1914 - 1 = 2,403 years. 1086 to 1215 is 129 years; 1517 to 1914 is 397.

courseCheck: A mixed set: classify sources for a stated question; source a short extract; compute intervals across the BCE/CE boundary and name centuries; place and order events on a timeline; sort the factors behind an event into conditions, causes and trigger; tell fact, evidence and interpretation apart; pick the best-qualified claim and the evidence that would weaken it; a self-rated recall of the method steps.
platformNeeds: timeline_explorer resolves years only. Lessons on 1914 and 1791 to 1804 need month and day (or a plain ordering card) for events inside one year: add optional month and day to events or use order_sequence as drawn. Each such figure uses order_sequence as the fallback.

Source-card figure: an extract with its provenance panel (author, date, audience, purpose) hidden behind taps, so the learner chooses which question to ask before seeing the answer. Fallback: table plus svg_figure.
Map figure for cases where place matters (Silk Roads, Mongol conquests, Atlantic trade): a deterministic SVG map with dated layers.
